text: Terrain-Aware UAV-Enabled Mobile Edge Computing in Urban Environments: A Constrained Multi-Objective Approach With Task-Adaptive Mechanism
Zexiong Wu , Qiqi Xie , Zhuoran Wang, Xumin Huang , Chaoda Peng , Member, IEEE, and Yuan Wu , Senior Member, IEEE

Abstract—With the increasing and multifaceted demands for wireless communication in smart cities, uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-enabled mobile edge computing (MEC) systems have garnered substantial interest due to their potential to enhance connectivity and computational capabilities. In these systems, UAVs are deployed to predetermined locations to establish communication with nearby user devices (UDs), thereby providing network coverage and computational offloading services. Nevertheless, the presence of complex urban terrains, including rough topographies and dense buildings, results in significant path loss in UAV-to-UD communication links and increases the risk of collisions during UAV navigation, ultimately degrading the quality of service (QoS) and compromising UAV operational safety. To mitigate these challenges, this study introduces a terrain-aware channel model capable of precisely evaluating the effects of terrain characteristics on UAVto-UD link performance. To improve QoS for UDs while ensuring UAV flight safety, we formulate a constrained multi-objective optimization problem (CMOP) to jointly optimize UAV trajectory, destination, and resource allocation, aiming to minimize task completion time and enhance UAV flight safety. To solve this CMOP, we propose a multi-task constrained multi-objective evolutionary algorithm with a task-adaptive mechanism, promoting the search for Pareto optimal solutions. Numerical results indicate that the proposed method outperforms baseline algorithms in achieving a well-converged set of feasible solutions with enhanced diversity.

I. INTRODUCTION

W ITH the emergence of smart cities, uncrewed aerialvehicle (UAV)-enabled mobile edge computing (MEC) vehicle (UAV)-enabled mobile edge computing (MEC) has attracted considerable attention due to its unique advantages, such as high mobility, flexibility, and an increased likelihood of establishing line-of-sight (LoS) links [1], [2]. These attributes enable UAVs to perform critical tasks in urban environments, particularly where traditional ground-based infrastructures are prone to failure or inefficiency [3]. For instance, UAVs can rapidly establish temporary communication networks in areas with poor connectivity [4]. Moreover, they can be deployed across various urban zones to collect real-time data, assisting in traffic management [5], air quality monitoring [6], and public safety surveillance [7]. In these scenarios, ensuring optimal quality-of-service (QoS) and effective path planning becomes crucial, since they directly impact the efficiency and reliability of UAV-enabled services in smart cities.

Enhancing the QoS for user devices (UDs) is a critical issue in UAV-enabled MEC systems within smart cities [8]. Task transmission delay depends on the signal strength of UAV-to-UD links and is a key determinant of QoS [9]. Therefore, accurate modeling of the signal strength is crucial in urban environments. Numerous studies have proposed various path loss channel models for evaluating UAV-to-UD links, which can be broadly categorized into three types, including statistical-based, radio map-based, and geographic information-based models [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]. The statistical-based models rely on empirical parameters to estimate the average signal strength, offering a computationally efficient and simplified approach [10], [11], [12]. However, they are practically inaccurate because they do not explicitly model the signal strength under the blockage of buildings and other urban structures, resulting in an inability to accurately account for non-line-of-sight (NLoS) conditions [15]. The radio map-based models utilize offline measurement data to train predictors, effectively estimating the impact of obstacles on UAV-to-UD links [13]. Despite their potential to capture detailed

The geographic information-based models leverage geometric relationships to infer LoS/NLoS conditions and directly estimate the average signal strength. While these models provide a more detailed representation by considering spatial relationships, they rely on the assumption of flat topography, neglecting natural variations in urban environments such as elevation differences. This oversimplification results in inaccurate signal strength estimates and ultimately compromises QoS.

Another critical issue in UAV-enabled MEC scenarios within smart cities is enhancing UAV flight safety [16]. Ensuring flight safety is essential to prevent potential injuries to personnel and damage to equipment resulting from collisions [17]. To achieve collision-free trajectories, extensive research has focused on developing UAV flight models. One common approach involves restricting UAV flight areas, such as limiting the flight altitudes above buildings [18]. While effective, these restrictions can limit the availability of collision-free paths outside designated zones. Moreover, during urgent missions, UAVs need to navigate through high-risk areas where such restrictions are impractical [19]. Another group of studies have concentrated on designing and optimizing metrics to identify the safest UAV flight paths [20]. However, these studies typically assume predetermined initial and final positions while designing collision-free trajectories between them. It is important to note that there have been several research efforts focusing on optimizing the destination position to improve communication efficiency between UAVs and UDs [21]. Nevertheless, these works overlook safety considerations. In practical urban scenarios, optimizing the final position itself can significantly enhance flight safety.

To address the two issues of accurately estimating the path loss on complex urban terrains and ensuring UAV flight safety, we propose a terrain-aware channel model. The model can estimate the signal strength under the blockage of urban terrains, including topographies and buildings, by utilizing data such as digital elevation model (DEM) data. By identifying topography and buildings near a UD, our terrain-aware channel model enables the division of space into two regions, namely, the region where the UAV-to-UD link is visible, and the blocked region where the UAV-to-UD link is obscured by the terrain. The blocked region is defined by a series of vectors shaped by the terrain around the UD, where the vectors are extending from the UD position to surrounding terrain points. This vector-based representation enables the propagation conditions and signal strength of the UAV-to-UD link to be inferred based on the Euclidean distance between the UAV and the blocked region. To develop an optimal solution for addressing the two issues, we formulate a constrained multi-objective optimization problem (CMOP) by jointly optimizing UAV trajectory, UAV destination, and resource allocation, aiming at improving QoS for UDs while ensuring UAV flight safety. Solving a CMOP requires effective algorithms capable of finding a set of Pareto optimal solutions while satisfying all constraints [22]. Evolutionary algorithms are popular choices for addressing various CMOPs and have been widely applied across numerous domains due to their inherent advantages, such as ease of implementation and robust global optimization capabilities [23]. The overall performance of these algorithms significantly depends on the selection of genetic operators, since these operators are crucial for effectively finding Pareto optimal solutions [24]. To tackle the CMOP studied in this paper, we propose a multi-tasking constrained multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (CMOEA) with a task-adaptive mechanism to seek superior solutions. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

To accurately estimate the signal strength, we design a terrain-aware channel model. Unlike existing blockage-aware channel models that assume simple terrains with flat topographies, our proposed model can identify blockages caused by complex terrains. This capability makes it applicable to a wider range of urban environments, offering greater flexibility and broader applicability.

This mechanism can retain historically effective genetic operators and adaptively assigns different genetic operators to individuals based on their specific tasks during the evolution process, thereby enhancing the search capability and convergence performance of the proposed algorithm. II. RELATED WORK

In this section, we present a review of two fundamental aspects in UAV-enabled MEC systems, namely, the path loss channel models and UAV trajectory design for flight safety. We conclude by identifying critical challenges in current research, which motivate our proposed solution.
A. Path Loss Channel Models

In this subsection, existing path loss channel models are classified into three distinct categories based on their methodological approaches for inferring propagation conditions and estimating average signal strength.

Statistical models are commonly used to assess the average performance of communication channels [14]. These models characterize propagation conditions using empirical channel parameters obtained from statistical measurements. Given specific channel parameters and a UAV-UD position pair, they can directly estimate the average signal strength. For example, probabilistic LoS channel models that incorporate parameters related to LoS and NLoS conditions have been utilized to predict the average signal strength of UAV-to-UD links [11], [25]. These models are widely applied in hierarchical computing frameworks, where the next-generation wireless networks (6G) are leveraged to aggregate substantial computational resources to process the time-varying multi-modal data uploaded by UDs [26], [27]. However, these simplified statistical channel models are only suitable for analyzing average performance and may fail to provide satisfactory results for specific user equipments (UEs) in real-world environments [13]. In practice, terrain conditions such as buildings and other obstacles can obstruct air-to-ground (A2G) signals, significantly degrading the propagation environment, particularly in densely built urban areas [13].

Radio map-based channel models can accurately assess the impact of obstacles on signals and describe the average strength of UAV-to-UD signals [14]. These models require extensive channel measurement data to create a radio map using machine learning techniques. The goal is to train a channel predictor that determines the propagation conditions and estimates the signal strength for the UAV-to-UD link [13], [28]. In [28], a predictor for radio map reconstruction is developed by employing the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm to learn segments. Given a specific UAV-to-UD position pair, the trained predictor utilizes the radio map to determine the propagation conditions and estimate the signal strength. However, due to the difficulty of obtaining sufficiently accurate channel quality assessments for possible combinations of UAV-UE 3-D positions, practical applications of radio maps are challenging [14].

Geographic information-based channel models can identify LoS/NLoS conditions and predict the average signal strength by evaluating A2G links obstructed by buildings [14]. These models can construct a blocked region for a UD by using basic geometric principles and geographic information [15]. By computing the distance between UAV and blocked region, the propagation conditions and signal strength can be inferred. Particularly, when a UAV hovers outside the blocked region, the distance between UAV and blocked region is positive, which can judge the propagation conditions as LoS. In [29], a distance-based weighted sum method is designed to improve the estimation performance of blockage-aware channel models by exploiting the fine-grained structure of propagation conditions. However, these studies typically assume a simple urban terrain with flat topography. In practical urban scenarios, rough topography can significantly affect the signal strength of UAV-to-UD links [30].
B. Trajectory Design for UAV Flight Safety
In this subsection, we categorize the existing methods for designing UAV flight trajectories into two distinct groups based on their approaches to achieving safe flight paths.

Several studies have focused on obtaining collision-free UAV flight trajectories by restricting the UAV flight area [15], [31]. In [32], an optimization problem is formulated to minimize task completion time while satisfying the minimum data demand of each user, under the assumption that the minimum flight altitude of the UAV exceeds the height of the tallest buildings. In [33], the flight area was predefined to ensure UAV flight safety near buildings. Following this, a joint optimization of transmission power, computation frequency, and duration is performed to minimize UAV energy consumption and task completion time. However, the assumption of a restricted UAV flight region in these studies can sacrifice potential low-altitude collision-free flight trajectories.

Some research incorporates UAV flight safety as an optimization objective or constraint to achieve collision-free UAV flight paths [34]. In [16], [34], collision avoidance constraints are used to ensure that the distance between the UAV and buildings is greater than a predefined value, resulting in a safe UAV flight trajectory. In [20], an optimization objective that represents the number of potential threatening terrain points near the UAV is constructed. By optimizing this objective while considering UAV dynamic constraints regarding turning angle, feasible solutions can be obtained to form safe and smooth UAV flight trajectories. However, these studies typically assume predefined initial and final positions for the UAV flight. In practical urban scenarios, the location of the UAV destination can also affect flight safety.
C. Critical Analysis of the Literature Review

Based on the above analyses of existing research, we identify two critical challenges in current UAV-enabled MEC systems. First, existing path loss channel models exhibit limited applicability in complex urban environments due to their reliance on extensive data collection or oversimplified terrain assumptions. Second, while various approaches have been proposed for UAV trajectory optimization, the impact of destination selection on both communication performance and flight safety remains largely unexplored. To address these challenges, we propose a comprehensive solution framework. For accurate signal strength estimation, we develop a terrain-aware approach utilizing real-world data, which systematically constructs blocked regions through an iterative integration process. To enhance both communication efficiency and operational safety, we design a safety-enhanced flight model based on the B-spline curve, enabling joint optimization of UAV trajectory and destination. These innovations lay the foundation for our subsequent problem formulation and algorithm design, which will be detailed in the following sections.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, we consider a UAV-enabled MEC system that operates under the control of a ground base station. The ground station performs global trajectory planning where a UAV navigates from an initial position to an optimized destination while maintaining collision-free trajectory. Upon reaching its destination, the UAV establishes a hovering position to receive and process computational tasks from nearby UDs according to the pre-planned resource allocation scheme. E. Problem Formulation

In this study, we focus on optimizing the performance of UAV-enabled MEC in smart cities by addressing two critical challenges: ensuring accurate signal strength estimation in complex urban environments and maintaining UAV flight safety. We formulate a joint optimization framework that considers both UAV trajectory planning and computational offloading decisions. Specifically, we aim to simultaneously minimize two objectives: the UAV flight safety risk (denoted as $G _ { 1 } )$ and the maximum task completion time of UDs (denoted as $G _ { 2 } )$ .

It is worth noting that there is a conflict between optimizing $G _ { 1 }$ and $G _ { 2 }$ as improving the latter requires the UAV to hover near the UD which, in turn, brings it close to the surrounding terrain and reduces flight safety. To handle different tradeoffs between these two conflicting objectives, we model the joint optimization of UAV trajectory planning and computational offloading as a CMOP, where we optimize the UAV trajectory, destination selection, and computational resource allocation while satisfying constraints on UAV flight safety, UAV kinetics, and computational resources. We define a decision variable vector as $\mathbf { x } = \{ \mathbf { U } _ { 1 } , \mathbf { U } _ { 2 } , \ldots , \mathbf { U } _ { \lambda } , f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots , f _ { I } \}$ . $$
\min \left\{ \begin{array}{l} G _ {1} (\mathbf {x}), \\ G _ {2} (\mathbf {x}), \end{array} \right.
$$

First, we review the fundamental concepts of constrained multi-objective optimization to establish the necessary background. Subsequently, we elaborate on the genetic encoding scheme for representing decision variables in our algorithm. Finally, we present the proposed algorithm along with the taskadaptive mechanism.
A. Representation of the Genetic Encoding Scheme

The solution to Problem (23) is encoded as a float individual, as shown in Fig. 3. An individual is divided into two parts. The first part (denoted as $u n i t _ { 1 } )$ is $\{ \mathbf { U } _ { 1 } , \mathbf { U } _ { 2 } , \dots , \mathbf { U } _ { \lambda } \}$ , where $\mathbf { U } _ { l }$ is a float variable representing the l-th control point of the constructed B-spline curve that determines the UAV trajectory. The second part (denoted as unit2) is $\{ f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots , f _ { I } \}$ , where $f _ { i }$ is a float variable representing the computing resource assigned from UAV to task of the i-th UD. B. Core Algorithm Design

To obtain the Pareto optimal solutions for Problem (23), we propose a multi-tasking CMOEA. The proposed algorithm serves as a global trajectory planning and resource allocation mechanism, which is executed at the ground base station before the UAV’s mission starts. Given the comprehensive environmental information including DEM data and UD distributions as inputs, our algorithm generates a complete flight trajectory from the initial position to an optimized destination, along with the corresponding resource allocation scheme for computational tasks. When the UAV destination $\mathbf { U } _ { \lambda }$ is positioned in close proximity to the UDs, the signal gain $g _ { i } ( \mathbf { q } ^ { \mathrm { U } } )$ of the UAV-to-UD ( )links can be significantly enhanced, thereby reducing the task completion duration. However, this proximity to UDs inherently brings the UAV closer to surrounding terrain features. Such positioning introduces potential hazards to UAV flight safety and increases the probability of UAV-to-UD links experiencing NLoS conditions, which consequently diminishes communication efficiency. In response to these challenges, our algorithm is meticulously designed to ensure the UAV can navigate safely and smoothly from its initial position to an optimal destination, maintain position near UDs while preserving LoS propagation conditions, and efficiently allocate limited computing resources across UDs to achieve superior computational performance. This comprehensive global planning methodology seamlessly integrates terrain-related constraints, safety requirements, and QoS objectives throughout the optimization process. As a result, it delivers highly efficient and reliable UAV operations in the urban environments.

The proposed algorithm operates with two cooperative populations to enhance its search capability: a main population and an auxiliary population. In CMOP1 and CMOP2, despite the confined UAV path planning area, our algorithm achieves consistent improvements over the baseline methods. C. Investigation of the Task-Adaptive Mechanism

To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed task-adaptive mechanism, we conduct comparative experiments on CMOP2 using two algorithm configurations: one incorporating the taskadaptive mechanism (denoted as “Yes”) and another using the original genetic operators (denoted as “No”). The original genetic operators utilize the DE/current-to-rand/1 operator and polynomial mutation. Table IV presents the comparative results, demonstrating the significant impact of the task-adaptive mechanism.

Our task-adaptive mechanism significantly enhances algorithm performance through genetic operator coordination. This mechanism intelligently selects and applies genetic operators based on historical performance data, dynamically matching operators to specific solution characteristics. Through experimental validation, we demonstrate its effectiveness with a 19.0% reduction in mean IGD value and a 32.2% increase in mean HV value compared to the original genetic operators. The mechanism achieves an optimal balance between exploration and exploitation through three complementary mutation operators: the first creates smoother trajectories by enhancing similarity between control points, the second explores potential feasible trajectories through strategic randomized control point generation, and the third applies polynomial mutation with precisely controlled perturbations to navigate the solution space efficiently. By recording and reapplying effective genetic operators that worked well on similar individuals, the proposed algorithm effectively balances between discovering promising solution regions and refining solutions in these areas, thereby enhancing its capabilities in balancing flight safety and communication efficiency requirements.
VI. CONCLUSION

In this study, we investigated a UAV-enabled MEC system operating in complex urban environments, where rough topographies and dense buildings pose significant challenges to both UAV-to-UD communication links and flight safety. Our contributions are threefold: First, we proposed a terrain-aware channel model that effectively evaluates the impact of complex urban terrain on UAV communication performance by systematically constructing blocked regions through an iterative integration process. Second, we formulated a CMOP that jointly optimizes UAV trajectory, destination position, and resource allocation to balance QoS enhancement and flight safety. Third, we developed a multi-tasking CMOEA with a task-adaptive mechanism that dynamically assigns genetic operators based on solution characteristics.

Our comprehensive experimental results demonstrated the superior performance of the proposed algorithm across three test scenarios of increasing complexity, achieving approximately 70.2% reduction in mean IGD and 77.5% increase in mean HV compared to baseline algorithms. The ablation studies validated the effectiveness of our task-adaptive mechanism, which improved performance by 19.0% in IGD and 32.2% in HV by intelligently leveraging historical information about effective genetic operators. Additionally, our terrain-aware channel model proved significantly more accurate than the probabilistic LoS channel model, achieving practical LoS probabilities of 95.63% compared to 63.45% with traditional approaches.
